name: Chronophotograph
basis: why: one plate exposed again and again, a bright figure adds light wherever it goes; how: past exposures laid down keeping the brighter value

lumenary.blurb: Étienne-Jules Marey’s way of seeing motion: a single plate, exposed again and again, so every moment of a movement stays on the picture at once. A video leaves a trail of its own past. A still picture is sent across the plate to show the idea.

facts.era: Marey’s photographic gun of 1882 and fixed-plate work after it
facts.bestOn: A bright subject moving across a dark background

why: Before film, nobody could say exactly what a galloping horse’s legs were doing. Marey answered by exposing one plate again and again, so that every instant of a movement lay on the same picture. It works because a bright figure on a black ground adds light to the plate wherever it goes and takes none away. Strobe photography still does the same, and the result shows time as a shape.
how: Turn each frame into what goes on the plate: a toned picture with the background pushed towards black.
Every fraction of a second, keep a copy of the current frame in a ring of past exposures.
Lay the exposures down from the oldest to the newest, each dimmer the older it is, always keeping the brighter value.
On video, optionally find what moves by comparing with the still background, and lay down only that.
On a still picture, slide a smaller copy across the plate on a swinging path, so there is motion to record.
Add a faint measuring grid and a dark vignette like a laboratory plate.
history: Étienne-Jules Marey, a French physiologist, wanted to measure how bodies move. In 1882 he built a camera shaped like a gun that took twelve exposures a second on one rotating plate, and soon after he moved to a fixed plate with a single lens, dressing his subjects in black with white lines on the limbs so that their paths showed as lines. His pictures influenced the Futurists and Duchamp’s Nude Descending a Staircase (1912). Harold Edgerton’s flash photographs, from the 1930s, brought the method into modern science and the studio.
uses: Title cards for films about motion
terms: Photography that records the successive phases of a movement, on one plate or in a series of pictures.
A light that flashes at regular intervals, freezing a moving subject in each flash.
Combining two pictures by keeping, at each pixel, the brighter of the two values.
paragraphs: The plate is a running maximum. Every exposure is a copy of the picture with its background crushed, E = l^0.92 smoothstep(a, a + 0.4, l) tinted silver or sepia, where l is the brightness and a is the black point (0 to 0.55). The newest exposure has weight 1 and one that is j exposures old has weight (1 - j/K)^x, with K the number of exposures and x between 0.35 and 3.2 from the fade slider. The plate is P = max over j of w_j E_j, taken for each colour channel, which is exactly what a second flash does to a film that already holds an image: it can only add light.

A new exposure is stored every g milliseconds from the latest video frame, so the exposures are g apart. A still picture has no past to store, so it is shrunk to half size, given a soft oval edge, and moved on a path x(t) = 0.29 W sin(1.3 t) with a small bounce 0.03 H sin(2.6 t + 0.8); the exposures are the same picture at earlier points on that path. In the mode that keeps only what moves, the still background is found as the per-pixel median of the newest frame, one from the middle of the trail and the oldest; each exposure is mixed in where it differs from that background by more than 22 levels, and the background itself is dimmed by half.

equations.note: An exposure with its background crushed, and the weight of an exposure that is j steps old.
The plate keeps the brightest value that any exposure gave, in each colour channel.
The path a still picture is swung along, so that there is motion to record.

presets.text: More exposures with a long gap draw the whole swing as a fan of figures.
Keep colour and the background for a pastel strobe look.
On video, laying down only what moves keeps the room and leaves ghosts of the people.
